steps.say: Surgery for reflux is only offered when reflux is proven and medicines have failed or a large hernia is present. A Nissen wrap goes all the way around the oesophagus, a full 360-degree wrap, and it works best when the gullet still squeezes normally. When the squeeze is weak, surgeons choose a Toupet, a 270-degree partial wrap at the back, so food can still pass. Every patient needs manometry and pH testing first, because operating on the wrong diagnosis is the commonest cause of a bad result.
steps.tx: **Nissen fundoplication** (complete 360-degree wrap of stomach around the lower oesophagus) is offered for proven reflux with a large hiatus hernia, refractory oesophagitis (persistent inflammation despite treatment) or troublesome regurgitation. A **Toupet** 270-degree posterior partial wrap suits **weak peristalsis** (poor oesophageal squeeze), because a full wrap in that setting causes severe swallowing difficulty. Manometry (pressure study) and pH-impedance testing confirm reflux and grade motility before surgery.

vis.alt: Panels showing endoscopy, barium swallow and manometry findings used to work up dysphagia and reflux before antireflux surgery.
vis.caption: Dysphagia workup with endoscopy, barium swallow and manometry guides wrap choice. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Barrett means the normal pale lining of the lower oesophagus has been replaced by red columnar lining, and the biopsy shows gut type cells with goblet cells. You need at least 1 cm of that lining to call it Barrett, because tiny tongues without goblet cells carry almost no cancer risk. Once Barrett is confirmed, the dysplasia grade drives everything. No dysplasia means watch it, while dysplasia means remove it endoscopically.
steps.tx: **Barrett oesophagus** (columnar lining replacing squamous lining from chronic reflux) needs biopsy proof of **intestinal metaplasia** (gut-type cells with goblet cells) in at least **1 cm** of columnar lining above the junction. Shorter tongues of columnar change without goblet cells do not count as Barrett. The **dysplasia grade** (none, low or high) then decides between continued surveillance and **endoscopic eradication** (ablation or resection of the abnormal lining).

vis.alt: Five stages from normal oesophagus through GERD and Barrett to invasive adenocarcinoma with endoscopy and histology views.
vis.caption: GERD to Barrett to adenocarcinoma sequence drives surveillance and eradication. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Timings matter more than anything in Barrett follow up. With no dysplasia, a scope every 3 to 5 years is enough, because progression is slow. Low grade disease comes back every 6 to 12 months, and any nodule is lifted and snared off. High grade disease is treated rather than watched, with nodule resection followed by radiofrequency ablation of everything that remains.
steps.tx: Surveillance intervals follow dysplasia. **Nondysplastic Barrett** (no abnormal cells) is scoped every **3 to 5 years**. **Low-grade dysplasia** (mildly abnormal cells) is surveyed every **6 to 12 months**, with eradication offered for persistent or nodular disease. **High-grade dysplasia** (severely abnormal cells still above the basement membrane) gets **endoscopic mucosal resection** (lifting and snaring of visible nodules) plus **radiofrequency ablation** (controlled heat destroying the flat Barrett segment).

rows: Scope every 6 to 12 months, resect nodules
Resect nodules plus ablate flat segment

steps.say: The LINX is a bracelet of magnets that sits around the lower sphincter and stops acid coming up while letting food go down. It suits patients with a small hernia and a normally squeezing oesophagus, particularly those who want to keep the ability to belch. It has no place with a big hernia, badly ulcerated lining or nickel allergy. Fundoplication remains the answer in those patients, because magnets cannot fix a wide anatomical defect.
steps.tx: **Magnetic sphincter augmentation** (LINX device, a ring of magnetic beads around the sphincter) suits reflux with a small hernia and normal motility, especially when the patient wants to preserve belching and vomiting. It is avoided with a large **hiatus hernia** (wide diaphragmatic defect), severe **oesophagitis** (deep ulcerated inflammation) or **nickel allergy** (immune reaction to the metal), where fundoplication remains the safer choice. Dysphagia after LINX usually settles, but persistent cases need dilation or removal.

steps.say: When a wrap fails, the patient returns with one of three complaints, burning coming back, new trouble swallowing, or bloating with no ability to belch. Do not rush back to theatre on symptoms alone. Repeat the manometry and the pH study first, because a slipped wrap needs redo surgery while a missed motility disorder needs a completely different operation.
steps.tx: A **failed fundoplication** (wrap that no longer controls reflux) presents with recurrent heartburn, new dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) or **gas-bloat** (trapped wind with inability to belch). Slipped, disrupted and misplaced wraps give different pictures, so **redo fundoplication** (repeat wrap surgery) needs full retesting first. Oesophageal **manometry** (pressure study) plus pH-impedance testing separates true wrap failure from a wrong initial indication such as missed achalasia.

steps.say: A paraoesophageal hernia turns deadly when the stomach twists inside the chest and nothing can get through. The triad to memorise is pain high in the belly, dry retching that brings nothing up, and a stomach tube that simply will not pass. That combination means complete obstruction, so stop fiddling with the tube and get the patient to theatre for urgent reduction and fixation.
steps.tx: **Paraesophageal hernia** (stomach rolling beside the oesophagus into the chest) with **gastric volvulus** (twisting of the stomach) is a surgical emergency. **Borchardt triad** (three classic signs) pairs severe epigastric pain with fruitless retching and a **nasogastric tube** (tube through the nose into the stomach) that refuses to pass, marking complete obstruction. Stop tube attempts at once; arrange urgent reduction with sac excision and fixation, because ischaemia and perforation follow delay.

nodes.label: Borchardt triad: pain, dry retching, tube will not pass
Stop: urgent contrast study if stable
Reduce stomach, excise sac, fix plus wrap

steps.say: Years of reflux scar the oesophagus short, and the stomach springs back into the chest the moment you let go. The intraoperative test is simple, you must have 2 to 3 cm of gullet lying relaxed below the diaphragm. If it will not stay, fashion a Collis tube from the top of the stomach to gain length, then wrap around that. A partial wrap is safer here, because a full wrap on a stiff gullet causes obstruction.
steps.tx: A **short oesophagus** (gullet scarred and tethered so it will not stay in the abdomen) is diagnosed when only **2 to 3 cm** of relaxed intra-abdominal oesophagus can be secured without traction. Dragging the junction down by force guarantees wrap disruption and later recurrence. A **Collis gastroplasty** (stapled lengthening procedure on the stomach) builds a gastric tube that extends the gullet, letting the fundoplication sit without tension, and is paired with a partial wrap to limit postoperative dysphagia.

steps.say: Closing the hiatus with stitches is enough for most hernias, so mesh is kept for the exceptions. Use it when the hole exceeds 5 cm or when you are redoing a repair in scarred tissue. Choose a biologic or absorbable mesh, because a permanent plastic mesh sitting against the gullet can erode into it years later. Routine mesh in small hernias causes harm without evidence of benefit.
steps.tx: **Mesh cruroplasty** (reinforcing the diaphragmatic crura with mesh) is reserved for hiatal defects over **5 cm** or redo repairs where native tissue is weak. **Biologic** (human or animal derived) or absorbable synthetic mesh is preferred, because permanent synthetic mesh at the hiatus risks **mesh erosion** (mesh working into the oesophageal wall) with fistula and stricture. Routine mesh for small primary defects adds cost and risk without proven benefit.
